title: EPA 608 Type II practice test
description: Free EPA Section 608 Type II (high-pressure appliances) practice questions. Every answer is explained and linked to the section of 40 CFR Part 82 it comes from.

questions.question: Under the EPA definition, a high-pressure appliance uses a refrigerant with a liquid phase saturation pressure in which range at 104 °F?
questions.explanation: The rule defines a high-pressure appliance by a refrigerant saturation pressure "between 170 psia and 355 psia at 104 °F." The range of 45 to 170 psia defines a medium-pressure appliance, and above 355 psia is part of the very high-pressure definition.

source.title: eCFR: 40 CFR 82.152, Definitions (as of Nov 3, 2026)

questions.question: Which refrigerant does the EPA definition list as an example for a very high-pressure appliance?
questions.explanation: The definition of a very high-pressure appliance lists R-13, R-23, R-503, R-508A and R-508B as examples. R-410A and R-22 are listed as high-pressure examples, and R-134a is listed as a medium-pressure example.

source.title: eCFR: 40 CFR 82.152, Definitions (as of Nov 3, 2026)

questions.question: Which refrigerant does the EPA definition list as an example for a high-pressure appliance?
questions.explanation: The high-pressure appliance definition gives R-22, R-407A, R-407C, R-410A and R-502 as examples. R-11 is listed under low-pressure, R-12 under medium-pressure and R-13 under very high-pressure appliances.

source.title: eCFR: 40 CFR 82.152, Definitions (as of Nov 3, 2026)

questions.question: Under the EPA definition, which of these jobs counts as major maintenance, service, or repair?

options.C: Uncovering an opening of 3 square inches of flow area for 10 minutes
options.D: Uncovering an opening of 2 square inches of flow area for 30 minutes

questions.explanation: Major repair includes any work that involves removal of the compressor, condenser, evaporator, or auxiliary heat exchange coil. An opening only counts if it is "more than four (4) square inches of 'flow area' for more than 15 minutes," so the 2- and 3-square-inch openings do not qualify.

source.title: eCFR: 40 CFR 82.152, Definitions (as of Nov 3, 2026)

questions.question: A person repairs high-pressure appliances (not small appliances, MVACs, or MVAC-like appliances). Which technician certification does 40 CFR 82.161 require?

options.D: Certification under 40 CFR part 82, subpart B only

questions.explanation: The rule says persons who work on medium-, high-, or very high-pressure appliances (except small appliances, MVACs, and MVAC-like appliances) "must be certified as Type II technicians." Type I covers small appliances and Type III covers low-pressure appliances.

source.title: eCFR: 40 CFR 82.161, Technician certification (as of Nov 3, 2026)

questions.question: A high-pressure appliance has a full charge of less than 200 pounds. Using recovery equipment manufactured on or after November 15, 1993, to what level must it be evacuated before opening?
questions.explanation: Table 1 lists 0 inches of Hg vacuum for a high-pressure appliance, or isolated component, with a full charge of less than 200 pounds, for equipment of either age. The 10-inch level applies to high-pressure appliances of 200 pounds or more.

source.title: eCFR: 40 CFR 82.156, Proper evacuation of refrigerant from appliances (as of Nov 3, 2026)

questions.question: A high-pressure appliance has a full charge of 200 pounds or more. Using recovery equipment manufactured on or after November 15, 1993, to what level must it be evacuated before opening?
questions.explanation: Table 1 sets 10 inches of Hg vacuum for a high-pressure appliance with a full charge of 200 pounds or more when the recovery equipment was made on or after November 15, 1993. The 4-inch level is for older equipment, and 25 mm Hg absolute is for low-pressure appliances.

source.title: eCFR: 40 CFR 82.156, Proper evacuation of refrigerant from appliances (as of Nov 3, 2026)

questions.question: A high-pressure appliance has a full charge of 200 pounds or more. Using recovery equipment manufactured before November 15, 1993, to what level must it be evacuated before opening?
questions.explanation: Table 1 lists 4 inches of Hg vacuum for a high-pressure appliance of 200 pounds or more when the recovery equipment was made before November 15, 1993. The 10-inch level applies only to equipment made on or after that date.

source.title: eCFR: 40 CFR 82.156, Proper evacuation of refrigerant from appliances (as of Nov 3, 2026)

questions.question: A technician uses recovery equipment manufactured on or after November 15, 1993, on a very high-pressure appliance. To what level must the appliance be evacuated before opening?
questions.explanation: Table 1 lists 0 inches of Hg vacuum for a very high-pressure appliance, with no split by charge size and the same level for equipment of either age. The deeper vacuum levels in the table apply to other appliance types.

source.title: eCFR: 40 CFR 82.156, Proper evacuation of refrigerant from appliances (as of Nov 3, 2026)

questions.question: A high-pressure appliance needs a repair that is not major, and it will not be evacuated to the atmosphere afterward. To what pressure must it be evacuated before it is opened?
questions.explanation: For non-major repairs not followed by evacuation to the atmosphere, a medium-, high- or very high-pressure appliance must be evacuated "to a pressure no higher than 0 psig before it is opened." The 5 psig level is only for oil changes.

source.title: eCFR: 40 CFR 82.156, Proper evacuation of refrigerant from appliances (as of Nov 3, 2026)

questions.question: For an oil change on a high-pressure appliance (a non-major repair, with no evacuation to the atmosphere afterward), to what pressure must the appliance be evacuated before it is opened?
questions.explanation: For oil changes, the appliance must be evacuated or pressurized "to a pressure no higher than 5 psig" before it is opened, or the oil can be drained into a system receiver brought to that level. The 0 psig level applies to other non-major repairs.

source.title: eCFR: 40 CFR 82.156, Proper evacuation of refrigerant from appliances (as of Nov 3, 2026)

questions.question: Leaks in a high-pressure appliance make it impossible to reach the Table 1 evacuation level. How far must the leaking components to be opened be evacuated?

options.A: To the full Table 1 level, with no exceptions
options.C: No evacuation is needed if the component is leaking
options.D: To the lowest level attainable without substantially contaminating the refrigerant, not above 0 psig

questions.explanation: When leaks make Table 1 levels unattainable, leaking components must be evacuated to the lowest level reachable without substantially contaminating the refrigerant, and "This level may not exceed 0 psig." Non-leaking components must still reach the Table 1 levels.

source.title: eCFR: 40 CFR 82.156, Proper evacuation of refrigerant from appliances (as of Nov 3, 2026)

questions.question: A technician may evacuate only the part of an appliance being serviced, instead of the whole appliance, if the refrigerant in that part can be isolated to what?
questions.explanation: The rule lets technicians evacuate either the entire appliance or the part to be serviced, "if the refrigerant in the part can be isolated to a system receiver." A system receiver is defined as the isolated portion or vessel of the appliance used to hold the charge during service.

source.title: eCFR: 40 CFR 82.156, Proper evacuation of refrigerant from appliances (as of Nov 3, 2026)

questions.question: System-dependent recovery equipment may not be used on appliances with a full charge of more than how many pounds, unless it is permanently attached as a pump-out unit?
questions.explanation: The rule says system-dependent equipment "may not be used with appliances with a full charge of more than 15 pounds" of refrigerant. The only exception is when it is permanently attached to the appliance as a pump-out unit.

source.title: eCFR: 40 CFR 82.156, Proper evacuation of refrigerant from appliances (as of Nov 3, 2026)

questions.question: How does the EPA define system-dependent recovery equipment?

options.A: Equipment that requires the assistance of components contained in an appliance to remove the refrigerant
options.B: Equipment that removes refrigerant without the assistance of components contained in the appliance
options.C: Equipment that reprocesses refrigerant to the specifications in appendix A
options.D: A device that closes automatically when hoses are disconnected

questions.explanation: System-dependent recovery equipment "requires the assistance of components contained in an appliance" to remove refrigerant. Equipment that works without the appliance's components is the definition of self-contained recovery equipment.

source.title: eCFR: 40 CFR 82.152, Definitions (as of Nov 3, 2026)

questions.question: Refrigerant recovered from a high-pressure appliance may be put into which of these without first being recycled or reclaimed?

options.A: An appliance owned by a different person
options.B: An MVAC owned by the same person
options.C: A cylinder to be sold to another contractor
options.D: Another appliance owned by the same person

questions.explanation: Recovered refrigerant may go back into the appliance it came from "or to another appliance owned by the same person" without recycling or reclaiming. The rule excludes MVACs and MVAC-like appliances from this allowance.

source.title: eCFR: 40 CFR 82.156, Proper evacuation of refrigerant from appliances (as of Nov 3, 2026)

questions.question: As of April 10, 2020, the appliance maintenance and leak repair rules in 40 CFR 82.157 apply to which appliances?

options.A: Appliances with a full charge of 50 or more pounds of any refrigerant, including substitutes alone
options.B: Appliances with a full charge of 50 or more pounds of a class I or class II refrigerant, or a blend containing one
options.C: Appliances with a full charge of more than 15 pounds of any refrigerant
options.D: All high-pressure appliances, regardless of charge size

questions.explanation: As of April 10, 2020, the section applies only to appliances with a full charge of 50 or more pounds of a class I or class II refrigerant or a blend containing one. It states the requirements "do not apply to appliances containing solely substitute refrigerants."

source.title: eCFR: 40 CFR 82.157, Appliance maintenance and leak repair (as of Nov 3, 2026)

questions.question: A comfort cooling appliance has a full charge of 50 or more pounds of a class I or class II refrigerant. Above what leak rate must the owner or operator repair it (or retrofit or retire it) under 40 CFR 82.157?
questions.explanation: Section 82.157 sets a "10 percent leak rate for comfort cooling appliances" and other covered appliances not in the commercial or industrial categories. The 20 percent rate is for commercial refrigeration and 30 percent is for industrial process refrigeration.

source.title: eCFR: 40 CFR 82.157, Appliance maintenance and leak repair (as of Nov 3, 2026)

questions.question: A commercial refrigeration appliance has a full charge of 50 or more pounds of a class I or class II refrigerant. Above what leak rate must it be repaired (or retrofitted or retired) under 40 CFR 82.157?
questions.explanation: The rule lists a "20 percent leak rate for commercial refrigeration equipment." The 125 percent figure is the threshold for the chronically leaking appliance report, not the repair trigger.

source.title: eCFR: 40 CFR 82.157, Appliance maintenance and leak repair (as of Nov 3, 2026)

questions.question: An industrial process refrigeration appliance has a full charge of 50 or more pounds of a class I or class II refrigerant. Above what leak rate must it be repaired (or retrofitted or retired) under 40 CFR 82.157?
questions.explanation: Section 82.157 sets a "30 percent leak rate for industrial process refrigeration equipment." The 10 and 20 percent rates belong to comfort cooling and commercial refrigeration, and 35 percent is not one of the leak rates listed in this section.

source.title: eCFR: 40 CFR 82.157, Appliance maintenance and leak repair (as of Nov 3, 2026)

questions.question: Refrigerant is added to a comfort cooling appliance (full charge of 50 or more pounds of a class I or class II refrigerant) that is over its allowed leak rate. No industrial process shutdown is involved and no extension applies. How long does the owner or operator have to identify and repair the leaks?
questions.explanation: Owners or operators must identify and repair leaks "within 30 days (or 120 days if an industrial process shutdown is required)" of the refrigerant addition. The 120-day period applies only when an industrial process shutdown is required.

source.title: eCFR: 40 CFR 82.157, Appliance maintenance and leak repair (as of Nov 3, 2026)

questions.question: A leak was repaired without evacuating an appliance covered by 40 CFR 82.157 (full charge of 50 or more pounds of a class I or class II refrigerant). Within how many days of the successful initial verification test must the follow-up verification test be done?
questions.explanation: A follow-up verification test "must be performed within 10 days of the successful initial verification test." When the appliance was evacuated for the repair, the 10 days can instead run from when it reaches normal operating characteristics and conditions.

source.title: eCFR: 40 CFR 82.157, Appliance maintenance and leak repair (as of Nov 3, 2026)

questions.question: A leak repair on an appliance covered by 40 CFR 82.157 (full charge of 50 or more pounds of a class I or class II refrigerant) required evacuating part of the appliance. When must the initial verification test be performed?

options.A: Before adding any refrigerant to the appliance
options.B: After the appliance has run at normal conditions for 30 days
options.C: Only after the next refrigerant addition

questions.explanation: For repairs that require evacuating the appliance or a portion of it, the initial verification test "must be performed before adding any refrigerant to the appliance." The rule defines the initial test as one done before refrigerant is added back.

source.title: eCFR: 40 CFR 82.157, Appliance maintenance and leak repair (as of Nov 3, 2026)

questions.question: A commercial refrigeration appliance with a full charge of 500 or more pounds of a class I or class II refrigerant has exceeded its allowed leak rate. It has no automatic leak detection system. How often must leak inspections be done?
questions.explanation: For commercial refrigeration and industrial process refrigeration appliances of 500 or more pounds, leak inspections are required "once every three months" until four quarters in a row show no leaking above the applicable rate. Once per calendar year applies to the 50-to-under-500-pound size and to comfort cooling appliances.

source.title: eCFR: 40 CFR 82.157, Appliance maintenance and leak repair (as of Nov 3, 2026)

questions.question: Unless otherwise specified, for how long must the records required by 40 CFR 82.157 (for appliances with a full charge of 50 or more pounds of a class I or class II refrigerant) be kept?

options.D: Only until the next leak inspection

questions.explanation: The recordkeeping paragraph says records "must be kept for at least three years in electronic or paper format, unless otherwise specified." Full charge records are an example of a longer period: they are kept until three years after the appliance is retired.

source.title: eCFR: 40 CFR 82.157, Appliance maintenance and leak repair (as of Nov 3, 2026)
